text: This closing lesson assembles everything the course has built, state vectors, single-qubit gates, CNOT, measurement probabilities, and shot-based sampling, into one small, complete, runnable simulator. Build this once by hand, and the gap between quantum computing theory and quantum computing software closes for good.

Six functions make up the whole core. initState sets up the all-zero starting state from Chapter 1. applySingleQubitGate is Lesson 24's index-pairing trick, applied to any Chapter 2 gate. applyCNOT is Chapter 3's CNOT logic, generalized to any pair of qubits. probabilities is the Born rule: square each amplitude. And simulateShot is Lesson 26's shot-sampling idea, implemented for real, using a random draw against the cumulative probabilities.

The real test is running a circuit this course already knows cold: H on qubit 1, then CNOT from qubit 1 to qubit 2, starting from ket-00. Running that through the core gives a final state vector of 0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071, probabilities of exactly 0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, and 2,000 simulated shots landing at 1,004 and 996 — close to, but not exactly, 1,000 and 1,000, precisely the finite-sampling behavior the previous lesson predicted. Every piece checks out against a result derived by hand three chapters ago.

This core deliberately stops at real-valued amplitudes and four gates — enough to prove the architecture, not enough for serious work. Production simulators like Qiskit's Aer or the one behind Q# do the same core job, but add full complex-amplitude arithmetic for gates like Y, S, T, and the rotations, heavy performance optimization, and noise models that deliberately mimic real hardware's errors. None of that changes the fundamental idea demonstrated here — it's the same state vector, the same index-pairing, the same shot sampling, just engineered at production scale.

That's the whole course: from the classical bit's limits, through single- and multi-qubit gates, circuit diagrams, teleportation and superdense coding, to a working simulator built from first principles by hand. Every result along the way was computed, checked, and now reproduced in real, running code.
